newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Crude oil prices in Asia hit five-year peak.
newsitem.headline: Crude oil prices in Asia hit five-year peak.

text.p: Benchmark North Sea Brent crude prices hit a fresh five-year peak on Wednesday in Asia supported by worries over tight stocks for heating oil.
The November Brent futures contract, trading on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), rose to $25.15 per barrel -- the highest level since the 1990/1991 Gulf War.

Oil traders said the new peak surpassed a high of $25.06 hit in London trading hours on Tuesday and has topped a rally that has seen prompt crude prices jump 57 percent from this year's low of $15.93.
The rally has been inspired by a number of factors, including delays in the implementation of the so-called Iraq oil-for-food accord with the United Nations.
"It's very difficult to see anything bearish in the market, now or in the near future," one trader, who declined to be named, said.
Wednesday's new high was inspired by data late on Tuesday which showed tight distillate stocks in the United States.
The American Petroleum Institute (API) said distillate stocks rose in the week ended 11 October a less-than-had-been-expected 673,000 barrels to 114.32 million barrels.
But more importantly, the data showed a fall in stocks in the key northeast of the United States, the world's biggest heating oil market.
Traditionally, stocks are growing strongly at this time of the year to prepare for the colder winter season when heating oil demand surges.
But the latest data showed that overall U.S. distillate stocks -- of which heating oil is a major part -- were 17.7 million barrels lower than during the same time in 1995.
In Europe, middle distillate stocks were 283.35 million barrels at the end of September, down 33 million barrels from a year earlier.
The API also said crude oil stocks fell 417,000 barrels last week to 301 million.
Traders pointed to the stalled Middle East peace process as another factor supporting oil prices.
In addition, fighting between rival Kurdish groups in northern Iraq -- seen as a proxy fight between Iraq and Iran -- was adding to the bullish tone, traders said.
Worries about potential disruption to supplies from the Middle East -- which sits on 65 percent of proved reserves -- tends to drive prices higher.
Brent reached $40.95 per barrel during the Gulf War when Iraq invaded Kuwait before being ousted by Allied forces later.

Traders said potentially the only bearish factor for crude markets had been worries the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries might agree to raise production quotas for 1997 when it meets in November.
But those worries were quashed in the past week when a Gulf source said OPEC, including lynchpin Saudi Arabia, had no plans to raise its current supply level of 25.033 million barrels per day.
"That's taken out one of the potentially bearish factors for the market," said a trader.
Futures prices on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) -- another benchmark -- were hovering just below five-year peaks of $25.70 per barrel.
Trading on the after-hours ACCESS system in Asia, November NYMEX crude was last traded at $25.46 per barrel.
